question.problem: Given that $h(x,y,z)=xyz,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂h}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =-(rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}z{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
